speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL FACILITIES IN HEAVILY POPULATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I make a brief statement about assistance for airports in heavily populated areas. The federal government has for many years assumed full responsibility for capital expenditures in connection with main line and other airports required to support scheduled air services in Canada. It has also provided cost sharing grants to assist in the development of local airports, and outright grants for airstrips in remote areas.
For some time it has been apparent that the policy of grants to local and remote airstrips needed review because of changes in costs and in requirements, as well as changes in technology. The Department of Transport has had this whole matter under intensive review for some months, and I hope soon to be in a position to make a general statement.
Meanwhile, because of problems at certain airports in heavily populated areas which have substantial traffic although they are not served by scheduled air lines, action has already been taken to improve local airports by provision of additional facilities. This has
taken place with regard to Sherbrooke and Hamilton-Mount Hope-airports. The government has today decided to take steps at once to meet urgent situations at Sarnia; at the Niagara regional airport at St. Catharines, and at the Waterloo-Wellington airport by providing additional facilities at these air fields as well. Officials of the department will be getting in touch with local officials in the next few days.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday on orders of the day I gave some of the reasons why the government had asked the hon. member for Red Deer to undertake at this time a journey of some two weeks to Africa. I stated that the hon. gentleman had spent some 15 years living in Ethiopia, one of the important countries with which Canada enjoys a very close relationship, and that in addition to having spent this length of time in Africa he has had an opportunity, such as perhaps no other mem-be of this house has enjoyed, of getting to know personalities in many of the governments of Africa. He has followed for a long time the evolutionary events of that emerging continent.
Supply-External Affairs
There are a number of matters which are of concern to Canada at this time in relation to some of the situations in certain African countries. Canada has a limited number of diplomatic missions in Africa and a limited number of missions where we have non-resident heads of mission. In the light of events which are of great concern to foreign communities all over the world, in the light of some of the problems which will face us on December 1 at the United Nations, and for other reasons, we felt it was in this nation's interests that we should take advantage of the services which I believe the hon. member for Red Deer is eminently qualified to perform in this area.
It was only in this light that he was asked to undertake a task which, I think, will have useful results. He will visit, at our request, the headquarters of the economic commission for Africa in Addis Ababa, a capital which he knows very well, having lived there for 15 years. He will have meetings with certain officials there including officials of the organization for African unity. Hon. members will recall that there was a very important conference of non-aligned states held in Cairo a few weeks ago, attended by representatives of many African countries. It was not constitutionally possible for Canada and for other countries not represented at that conference to send observers, yet it is of the utmost importance that we should have the fullest information placed directly at our disposal, in addition to information from other sources, so we can take the necessary steps and prepare for some important decisions which will have to be made very shortly, at the United Nations in particular.
I should like to point out that we are taking advantage of the presence in Africa of the hon. member for Red Deer for another purpose. Hon. members will recall the question which was put to me a few moments ago by one of the members for Halifax-
Which one?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
One of the very active and useful members of this house. This question, as others have done, underlined our concern for the safety of a number of Canadians resident in the Stanleyville area of the Congo where 800 hostages are being kept by the rebel forces in circumstances such that the Red Cross and other bodies have not been able to elicit satisfactory assurances as to their safety. I may say that in this total of 800 some 26 Canadians are included. The government is using every method

Supply-External Affairs it can to extricate these Canadians and, indirectly, others, from the regrettable and dangerous position in which they have been placed. I may say that the hon. member for Red Deer has a knowledge of this area and knows some of the personalities involved.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the hon. member for Red Deer will visit Stanleyville?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows he cannot visit Stanleyville. Even representatives of the Red Cross cannot visit Stanleyville. But I hope there are certain contacts which can be made, in the Congo and elsewhere, which may lead to satisfactory negotiations. At any rate that is our thought, and that is what we intend to do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask what cities and towns in the Congo it is expected the hon. member for Red Deer will visit?

I am sure he will go to the capital, but it may be he will go elsewhere for the purpose of making contacts which we believe, from his acquaintance, he may be able to establish. In any event, we shall certainly resort to every effort in order to ensure as far as possible the safety of these Canadians, as the people of Canada would expect this government to do.
On October 14 a message was sent to a number of the governments which are members of the conciliation commission of the organization for African unity. This message asked these governments to use their influence to ensure that the Geneva conventions of 1949 were observed in the Congolese dispute so the lives and safety of the civilians involved, including Canadian and other nationals, who are presently held in rebel territory could be preserved. This appeal was made because it was considered that the articles of all four Geneva conventions is pertinent to the task of the conciliation commission. These articles impose on all signatory countries, even on those not parties to the conflict, an obligation to ensure respect for the convention and for the lives and safety of persons not actually involved in the dispute, such as our residents in the Congo.
The hon. member for Red Deer is due to visit Kenya next Monday and Tuesday and we are arranging for him to call on the distinguished prime minister of that country, Mr. Kenyatta, who is the chairman of the O.A.U. conciliation commission and a key figure in efforts to ensure the safety of our people in the Congo. I very much hope that in addition
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).j
to other appeals which have been made to Mr. Kenyatta this personal appeal by one who, I understand, knows him, will reinforce the messages which have already been sent.
We also hope that while in Ethiopia the hon. member for Red Deer will be able to ask the government of Ethiopia, which is also a member of the conciliation commission, to support measures for the safety of our citizens in the Congo. We all recall that when the Emperor of Ethiopia, that gallant and distinguished head of state, came to Ottawa a few months ago it was apparent that the hon. member for Red Deer had a very special relationship with him. We hope that in the circumstances this relationship will help in solving the problem of these people who find their safety threatened in Stanleyville.
I should add that in addition to visiting Ethiopia and Kenya I hope the hon. member for Red Deer will be able to visit at least one other country. I believe it is proper for us from time to time to utilize the experience and ability of members of this house. We do so at the United Nations. We ask members to constitute themselves as members of the Canadian delegation at the United Nations. We send members to sessions of the United Nations as observers. We send members to other international conferences, and I believe the assignment given to the hon. member for Red Deer to visit certain key countries and key personalities in Africa is in the interests of the formulation of clear and desirable foreign policy in these particular situations. I believe the course we have followed is one which will commend itself to most reasonable people, and I have no hesitation in commending it to this committee.

I listened with great attention to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs had to say on this interesting subject. I think most members of this house are aware of the previous experience of the hon. member for Red Deer in Ethiopia for some length of time in the field of education. I think hon. members, particularly those who had the pleasure of seeing the film "Mr. Pearson", realize that there is a relationship between the hon. member for Red Deer and the Emperor of Ethiopia. I believe that as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just said, most reasonable members would go along with that. However, there are some other things which seem a little obscure in this whole situation, and I was wondering whether the minister would elaborate and elucidate a little more in respect of them.

In the first place, Mr. Chairman, it is my information that at the present time the hon. member for Red Deer is visiting Ghana, in fact is just leaving that particular country, and that his next stop is the new United Republic of Tanzania, formerly Tanganyika. The minister has said he will then be visiting Kenya, and after that it is my understanding that the hon. member for Red Deer will be paying a relatively brief visit to Ethiopia and then on to Cairo, in the United Arab Republic. It is my understanding that at no time is the hon. member for Red Deer visiting the Congo or anywhere near there. The minister has just told us that he will be some place in the Congo, and I wonder whether the minister would expand on that just a little more.
There is another question that I think arises in the minds of many people. As the minister has said, naturally when the interests of Canada and Canadian problems are involved-particularly the lives of Canadian missionaries in the Congo-certainly this house would want everything possible done to protect the lives of these very courageous people. I have had some experience in this field and realize that sometimes in the field of external affairs you have to do things indirectly that you cannot do directly. Nevertheless it seems strange to me that if in fact one of the objects of the mission of the hon. member for Red Deer is to help protect the lives and security of Canadian and other missionaries in the Congo, he would not be visiting some designated place in that area or even close to it, perhaps some of the adjoining states.
Another matter that comes to mind is this. The hon. member for Red Deer has had experience in certain parts of Africa, but it is my understanding from people who are also quite knowledgeable about that continent that though you may be well received in one part of Africa it does not necessarily follow that you are going to be received with open arms in other parts of Africa. While I have no doubt the hon. member for Red Deer will be more than welcome in Ethiopia, and perhaps in certain other places in Africa, this perhaps would not apply to all the countries he is intending to visit.
I realize that in Africa, and indeed in other parts of the world, the position held opens doors to persons of influence, but the hon. member for Red Deer is a private member of this house. True, he is the leader of a small group of members here, but he is not a member of the privy council or anything
Supply-External Affairs of that nature. It seems odd to me that there is not some senior member of the Department of External Affairs who has perhaps a wider and greater knowledge of Africa in general, if not in particular-and even Ethiopia-than the hon. member for Red Deer. We have a great many highly experienced senior members of the Department of External Affairs who have had experience in Africa, and it seems rather odd that one of these persons was not sent as a special representative of the government of Canada, rather than a member, albeit the leader, of one of the opposition parties in the House of Commons.
The minister dealt with this matter slightly in his remarks, but I do not think he has satisfied most of us completely. I mentioned this yesterday briefly and the minister replied, also briefly. I refer to the question as to what extent members of opposition parties should take part in the formulation of government policy, because this in fact ties the hands of opposition parties and in this respect perhaps makes them an even closer ally of the government. I understand this question was settled some time ago. I believe I mentioned 1945 yesterday, but the minister of course was correct when he said it was 1946, after the initial organization meeting of the United Nations in San Francisco when members of all the political parties in this house at the time formed the Canadian delegation.
The minister mentioned Hon. Mr. Bracken, but it is my understanding that really the procedure was instigated by Hon. Mr. Cold-well, namely that it would be unwise for members, and particularly leaders, of opposition parties to take part in the formulation of government policy because it would completely tie their hands in the House of Commons on that particular subject and perhaps even on other subjects when they were being debated. As a result the institution of parliamentary observers was put into effect at the United Nations, which system has of course been copied by a great many other countries.
Now that the minister, for reasons best known to himself-he has probably told us a good many of them-has selected the hon. member for Red Deer for this job, he has certainly departed from that policy, which subsequent governments have followed ever since 1946. I have already mentioned that a policy such as this would help tie the hands not only of the member concerned but of

If it was very clear that the hon. member for Red Deer had a complete and unequalled knowledge of all parts of Africa, particularly the Congo-because that is apparently one of the leading items of business for the hon. gentleman- we might stretch a point; but it seems clear that the experience of the hon. member for Red Deer is largely confined to Ethiopia and not particularly to the Congo or these other parts of Africa mentioned by the minister. Mr. Chairman, I want to make it clear, of course, that the hon. member for Red Deer is not formulating policy, any more than an observer who goes to the United Nations formulates policy. My hon. friend is quite correct; there are in the Department of External Affairs, in some of our missions and here at home, individuals with a very wide knowledge of and an expertise in African affairs. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly correct that there are many matters in the field of external affairs more important than the one the committee is now discussing, but it is also true that a very important matter is that of the relations between the government and parliament. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not been playing fair with parliament with respect to this whole question.
In the first place, yesterday there was an obvious attempt to avoid having to deal with this matter. Then when we got into committee and the government was unable to avoid dealing with the matter we were given answers which were not as completely frank and straightforward as we feel they should have been. The President of the Privy Council, who is a member of the cabinet and who was present with ten or a dozen other ministers, told us he knew nothing at all about it. Finally we managed to get the Secretary of State for External Affairs into the house and he admitted to us quite openly that the hon. member for Red Deer had been asked by the government to undertake this assignment in Africa. Then when the minister was asked whether there was an order in council in this regard and, if not, how were the hon. member's expenses being paid, the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, first of all, was in this very direct sentence:
X do not believe there was an order in council.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Nor was one necessary.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That is not what the minister said yesterday.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And that is what I am saying now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
What the minister said yesterday was:
I do not believe there was an order in council.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Then I asked the minister:
Then how are the expenses being paid?
The reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was:
The hon. gentleman will have to indicate what his expenses were, and they will be examined and the proper procedure will be observed.
I then asked:
Is there an understanding that the expenses will be paid?

The minister's reply was:
It would be very unfair to ask an hon. gentleman to undertake such a responsibility and pay the expenses himself.
Those exchanges, Mr. Chairman, are to be found at page 9754 of Hansard for yesterday, Wednesday, November 4. One can draw from that-one has to draw it; it is not there in clear language-that the expenses of the hon. member for Red Deer are being paid.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister now says there is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And I said that yesterday clearly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister did not say that yesterday. The minister said yesterday what is reported on the pages of Hansard-
That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: -and he should stick with what the record shows and not try to distort it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am reading the record.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member must not say that I am trying to distort things, because I am not trying to distort things. I will look at Hansard, but I understood that I clearly indicated this yesterday.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That is no point of order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know why my hon. friend says I am trying to distort it, because I am not trying to distort it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: There is no point of order. The minister is now trying to say what he indicated yesterday to the house; but I am telling the house what he actually said yesterday, and I am doing so not by way of paraphrasing it or by putting it in my own words but by reading his words.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
What the minister said was:
I do not believe there was an order in council.
Then he went on:
The hon. gentleman will have to indicate what his expenses were, and they will be examined and the proper procedure will be observed.
Supply-External Affairs
He did not tell us whether they would be paid or what the proper procedure would be, so I went on to ask:
Is there an understanding that the expenses will paid?
The hon. gentleman's answer was:
It would be very unfair to ask an hon. gentleman to undertake such a responsibility and pay the expenses himself.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
So I say, Mr. Chairman, that we are right back where we were before the Secretary of State for External Affairs lost his temper a moment ago; that one can draw from that exchange that the expenses are being paid, although it was not said so clearly.
When the minister answered my question in this regard on orders of the day today he said "Yes, and I said so yesterday". At any rate, Mr. Chairman, we now have it clear; the expenses of the hon. member are being paid. This whole matter could have been dealt with yesterday in a matter of two or three minutes had we had a couple of direct answers.
Now we have this situation. The minister says now in the midst of this present exchange that no order in council is necessary. Obviously, knowing the sections of the Senate and House of Commons Act to which I was referring when I asked my question on orders of the day, he would know that there is a part of the Senate and House of Commons Act which is headed "Independence of parliament". Section 10 of the act reads as follows:
Except as hereinafter specially provided:
(a)	no person accepting or holding any office, commission or employment, permanent or temporary, in the service of the government of Canada-
It has been made very clear today that the hon. member for Red Deer is out in Africa in the service of the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just in the same way as any ordinary member going to a conference is in the service of the government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The section goes on:
-at the nomination of the crown or at the nomination of any of the officers of the government of Canada, to which any salary, fee, wages, allowance, emolument, or profit of any kind is attached; and
(b)	no sheriff, registrar of deeds, clerk of the peace, or county crown attorney in any of the provinces of Canada,
is eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote therein.

Supply-External Affairs
Many members of this House of Commons have been on delegations of one kind or another. We all know that in order to have our expenses paid when we are on such delegations there either has to be a special vote containing some wording to make it clear that it does not violate this act, or there has to be an order in council covering the special case. Unless the minister can produce a vote in his estimates so worded as to provide for a private member of parliament to be sent on a special mission to Africa of the type the hon. member for Red Deer has been sent on, I submit there will have to be an order in council before the hon. gentleman's expenses can be paid. Otherwise he will have to forfeit his seat under the provisions of section 10 of the Senate and House of Commons Act.
They do it retroactively. They have done that before.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That is probably what they will do, yes. I do not mind their doing it so long as they tell us and are frank about it. Whether the government wants to choose a particular person to do a job for the government is for the government to decide. I am not questioning the policy. I think there are questions which could be asked about it. I think it is an awkward position in which the hon. member for Red Deer will find himself when he comes back to Canada as the leader of a party outside of the government, but that is for the government to decide.
What I am concerned about, Mr. Chairman-and let me pinpoint it-is this. The only reason I have entered this debate at all is because I think parliament cannot carry on unless there is the best of relationships between the executive and the members of the House of Commons. You do not get a good relationship when we are played with, as we were yesterday and as we have been today with respect to this matter. If it was formally decided by the minister or the cabinet before the hon. member for Red Deer went to Africa that this was going to be done, and if it is definitely the case, as it now seems to be from what the minister has said, that the hon. member was given an assignment or a job, why did the government not do it in a regular, formal way, and why did the minister not so inform the House of Commons? This is my concern, Mr. Chairman.
There are other angles. The hon. member for Oxford has raised some of them and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands raised one and may pursue it later.


But my concern is the proper relationship that should exist between cabinet ministers and members of the House of Commons and I submit we have not had that proper relationship in this instance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is usually very precise and generally very fair, although sometimes he may not realize that he overstates his case. I think in the very words he has quoted from the record yesterday he will see that I clearly indicated there was no question that the expenses of the hon. gentleman were going to be borne. In fact my hon. friend quoted my own words to that effect. Yet he says that if we had said that yesterday it would have resolved the matter. My hon. friend does not think I am so naive as to believe that that would resolve the matter. I have seen too many situations in this house, including some of the participations of my hon. friend, to fail to realize that he would not refrain from taking advantage of any occasion which would cause merriment to the treasury benches. I must say that on occasion I have enjoyed that merriment myself but I am not going to say that this is one of the occasions.
With regard to the section of the Senate and House of Commons Act to which my hon. friend has directed our attention I may say quite frankly, and I may be overly naive in this frankness, that when the question arose of asking the hon. gentleman to undertake this assignment it certainly never dawned on my mind, or in the mind of anyone with whom this matter was discussed, that this action was one that was open to the interpretation which my hon. friend is seeking to give. It must be clear that the hon. member for Red Deer is receiving no emolument and no allowances. He is only going to get his expenses and, as I indicated yesterday, it would be unfair to expect him to undertake this particular assignment if his expenses were not paid.
I have checked with the officials of the privy council office and have been told that unless there is a contractual relationship, which would involve the payment of an emolument or of an allowance or of a consideration, there is no question of an order in council at all. The procedures advised by the treasury officers have been followed. I had no relationship with these arrangements myself except to suggest to the hon. member for Red Deer some of the things that were in our minds with respect to the reasons for which he was going to Africa.

Our authority, of course, is clear with regard to a situation of this kind. In the formulation of foreign policy or in the administration of the department I believe I have the authority under the general powers of administration to utilize those instruments, and this my hon. friend acknowledges, which will enable me and my colleagues to make the necessary policy assessments in this kind of situation. I have presumed, and I am told this is correct, that we have this authority under the departmental item which includes as well an amount for travelling expenses.
As my hon. friend knows, from time to time we engage individuals to do particular jobs in the department. We engage international law lawyers, university professors, in the summer particularly. They are, if members of parliament, clearly within the purport of the two sections to which my hon. friend has referred, but section 16 is the relevant section which calls for the payment of moneys by Canada. If I remember correctly, I do not think my hon. friend referred to this section at all. There is no public money, within the meaning of that section, to be paid to the individual in question. All he is receiving is his expenses, for which he must make a proper accounting to the department. That is the situation.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to partake at length in this debate. The question has arisen whether or not this action is a violation of the Senate and House of Commons Act and I should like to speak very briefly on that point. As has been pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, there will be no payment by the government out of public funds for any fees, wages, allowances, etc. So this puts the whole matter, in so far as the payment of expenses is concerned, into the same category as the payment of expenses to members of the House of Commons who are appointed as delegates to various interparliamentary bodies.
If the argument that has been advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is valid, then I suggest that almost all members of the house are in violation of section 16 of the Senate and House of Commons Act. It is not by my choice that it is necessary for me to go into this matter at this time, but we know for example that the Canadian branch of the commonwealth parliamentary association is granted approximately $20,000 or $25,000 annually and out of that grant members of the House of Commons who go to the conferences, both regional and international, are paid their expenses for 20220-620}
Supply-External Affairs travelling and accommodation, plus a certain limited amount of money for certain out of pocket expenses.
With regard to those members who go to the United Nations as observers, I believe they are paid out of the funds of the Department of External Affairs. They are paid the actual amount of their travelling expenses from Ottawa to New York. In addition, accommodation is provided during their stay in New York and they are also paid something like $13 per diem for out of pocket expenses. This is true for the United Nations observers, for the commonwealth parliamentary association delegates, for the interparliamentary union delegates, for the NATO parliamentary delegates and in a number of other special cases such as the recent trip to NORAD and also to SAC. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we must accept the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that only actual travelling expenses will be paid in this instance, and certainly this is completely in line with the practice that has been followed in the case of a great many members of the house.
I do not wish to deal at length with some of the other allegations that have been made. I want to say, however, to those members who have suggested that the Social Credit party is probably going to be tied to Liberal government policy-
Oh, oh.
That is nothing new.
It always has been.

Mr. Chairman, if you can hear
me over the babbling of these hon. gentlemen-
Why do you deny it so strongly?
-I should like to say that the Social Credit party has always regarded its duty to Canada and Canadians as coming first-
Oh, oh.

-and these allegations of being tied to or allied with any other party are completely unfounded. If you can hear me, Mr. Chairman, over these rumblings and mumblings that are going on to my right, I should like to point out that we were subjected to this same kind of abuse by the hon. gentlemen who now occupy the government benches when we gave our support time after time to the Progressive Conservative government when they were in office. We gave the reasons for that.

Supply-External Affairs
When?

During the session of 1962. This policy has been followed regardless of which party the Canadian people happened to choose to occupy the government benches. I should like you to know also that the Canadian people generally have appreciated the measure of stability this party has given the last two parliaments. We do not intend to depart from that course, regardless of the insinuations or allegations that may be hurled at us.
I may say also, Mr. Chairman, that we are not impressed with these small time insinuations that are being made. As has been very well pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, there is a very critical situation in certain parts of Africa which requires not only the interest of but certain action by the government and by the parliament of this country. Surely, the purpose is quite obvious. These insinuations are to obtain some temporary political expedient and should be completely disregarded in view of the gravity of the situation. I do not want to get into all of this. I had no intention of taking part in this debate to defend anyone. However, when allegations are made that there may be a violation of the Senate and House of Commons Act to the extent that the hon. member for Red Deer has no right to sit in this house, I simply repeat that if this argument is valid then a majority of the members of this house who have at different times accepted money through one route or another from the public treasury to pay their expenses on trips to the United Nations, Europe, Africa or Asia in the course of the last 12 months, are in the same position. We do not, therefore, accept this allegation at all.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and I have just heard those of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) about the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), who is now in Africa as a delegate or ambassador of the federal government.
The minister stated yesterday that no one could represent Canada so well in Africa, inasmuch as the hon. member for Red Deer had greater experience concerning Ethiopia, and perhaps a few neighbouring countries, than anybody else in Canada. Granted, the hon. member for Red Deer did spend some 15 years in Ethiopia as the man in charge of the educational system. However, I feel the

minister could have found in the Canadian diplomatic corps, someone perfectly aware of what is happening in every African country.
Five or six day ago we learned that the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) has been in Africa for one month on behalf of the Canadian government. I wonder if he is selling three maple leaf flags on stickers for automobile bumpers.
Be that as it may, the Minister without Portfolio is in Africa. Why also send the hon. member for Red Deer? Could it be that the Minister without Portfolio is a useless member within the federal cabinet? We know that he obtained his post of minister merely because he fought Social Credit during the last federal election. Today why does the secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) appoint the hon. member for Red Deer as a double to the Minister without Portfolio in Africa?
The minister tells us: We have very restricted missions in Africa, and that is why we are sending the hon. member for Red Deer, and even in the Congo, where 800 people are kept as hostages, including 26 Canadians.
It should be noted that the hon. member for Red Deer does not speak French, while the language spoken in the Congo is not English but French. If the Minister without Portfolio was there, I would say that perhaps with his convictions, his stakes in this government, he might have some influence on political doings in the Congo. But no, we were told that the hon. member for Red Deer was going there.
Mr. Chairman, in those conditions, if it is decided that because the hon. member for Red Deer lived in Ethiopia for 15 years we will send him to the Congo or to some other African country where he had never gone before, I do not see why the Secretary of State for External Affairs could not send Mr. Michel Chartrand to represent the Canadian government in Castro's Cuba? Why not send Mr. Chartrand to Russia, for instance, where he would feel perfectly at home, where he has close friends and where he might perhaps get somewhere on behalf of the present Canadian government?
Mr. Chairman, it seems childish to me to give us such explanations. They should tell us frankly that the hon. member for Red Deer just has been done the favour of going on a visit to African countries at the expense of the Canadian people, because he and his group promised to support this government

until the next general election and to keep it in office. Then, the minister would be more honest with parliament.
It is not true.

I hear the hon. member for Cariboo say "It is not true". He knows himself that it is true, and he is the one who opened the door for that situation between the Liberals and his own group.

Mr. Chairman, we have had enough of those electoral manoeuvres. This has been going on since 1963. I am not a Conservative and I support neither the Liberal nor the Conservatives, but the Liberals are sure that thanks to the support of the Social Credit group led by the hon. member for Red Deer, they will remain in power. That is the main reason why the hon. member has been sent to African countries he has never seen in his life. He will be visiting countries whose language he does not even understand, the Congo, for instance, where French is spoken.
Moreover, I wonder why the people of Canada have to pay for the trip made by the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville. Why is a second representative being sent to Africa? What is the Minister without Portfolio doing in Africa at this time?
The Conservatives have forgotten to ask that, and so have other hon. members, but we all know that the minister has been visiting Africa for the past month. What is he doing there? If he is serving no useful purpose in Africa, he should be brought back to Canada to prevent him from being the shame of our country abroad.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What about the Minister without Portfolio?

Over here he stays quiet; over there he says too much. The hon. member for Red Deer does not say anything.

Mr. Chairman, I recognize that the hon. member for Red Deer has some of the qualities of a diplomat. What is keeping the present government from appointing him ambassador to some country or other, in Africa if need be? But let the government ask him to resign as a member of parliament.
A while ago mention was made that members of the opposition parties had been sent to the United Nations. Yes, that is true. One
Supply-External Affairs member of the Social Credit party, one member of our group was sent at intervals of six months, and each time there were two or three Conservative members and some ten Liberals. But when it comes to Africa, two are sent: the Minister without Portfolio and a member of the opposition, the leader of a minority party in the house. This is a feat never before witnessed in parliament. Can the minister give us examples of the appointment of Conservative members, or members of the New Democratic party, or other parties, who were delegated, under similar circumstances, anywhere in the whole wide world? We may have sent delegates to Formosa once, but I do not know under what auspices nor for what reason. At all events, I would not criticize the government for doing so at that time, for I am not even sure of the facts.
Mr. Chairman, they should stop treating us like a bunch of gapers. They should be frank with us instead of telling us fairy tales and cock-and-bull stories.
Let the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell us what it is all about. If he intends to appoint the hon. member for Red Deer ambassador in some country or other, let him appoint him right now and there will be no more questions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Does the hon. member consider it might be possible that the hon. member for Red Deer is there to keep an eye on the Minister without Portfolio, or vice-versa?

That is exactly what I said a moment ago. He is over there to check the other man or they are checking each other, I don't know which.

Mr. Chairman, let them stop stringing us a line. If they wish to appoint the hon. member for Red Deer as ambassador, if he has the required qualifications-if he has lived in Ethiopia for 15 years and if he wants to go back-let the Secretary of State for External Affairs say so frankly and appoint him ambassador to Ethiopia, to Emperor Haile Selassie-for he is an emperor-and let there be an end to the whole thing. Let them stop laughing at us in the house.
On the other hand, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs thinks that to keep his government in power he must absolutely use the good services of the hon. member for Red Deer; here again I wonder whether the method is very honest.

Supply-External Affairs
At any rate, we should get explanations as regards, not only the presence of the hon. member for Red Deer in Africa but also that of the Minister without Portfolio.
What is the Minister without Portfolio doing there?
Assuming the hon. member for Red Deer is there to see to the goodwill between the various African states, what is the Minister without Portfolio doing in Africa at the expense of the government? It is time that we know and that the minister gives us the information we want.
Jealousy.
Mr. Chairman, I hear some members to my right saying that I speak through jealousy. As usual, these people talk through their hats.

I welcome the opportunity of making a few remarks on this matter but I have no intention of taking the same approach as the hon. member for Oxford, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Medicine Hat or the hon. member for Villeneuve. In their own way they have all raised most important matters regarding constitutionality, irregularity, payments to members of the house on this kind of job, and implied conspiracy between one party and another.
I do not want to discuss those angles because people better qualified than myself have already done so. Personally I wish the hon. member for Red Deer well during his three weeks in Africa. With his experience and contacts I hope he is able to do what is expected of him and what was anticipated of him when he was appointed to do this job. I hope he can bring back the information which the Secretary of State for External Affairs desires, and I think I would be less than honest if I failed to say that.
However, I would like to have the reasons behind such an appointment explained to me. I find it difficult to understand what kind of African bureau must exist in the Department of External Affairs. I find it difficult to understand that in that bureau there are not those with sufficient experience and knowledge to tackle this kind of job. I am not referring to the hon. member for Red Deer on a personal basis, but I am interested in what kind of advice the minister got when making this appointment. I do not pretend to be an expert on Africa, but in 1960 I had the privilege of attending the United Nations for six weeks,

and there meeting a great many African ambassadors, delegates and officials.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And the hon. member knows something about the situation in Africa too.

Eighteen months ago I had the opportunity of being with the commonwealth parliamentary association in Africa for six or seven weeks, and one thing I noted, both at the United Nations and in Africa, is that the African people in emerging nations have something which perhaps we as whites cannot appreciate, a prestige consciousness which gives them a certain psychological attitude. You go to Washington, you go to the United Nations, and the emerging African nations have such a sense of prestige consciousness they have to rent or own the most expensive homes; they have to own the most expensive cars; they demand diplomatic immunity as no other nation ever does. Here in our Commons area I believe there is only one car with a chauffeur, and that is for the Prime Minister. I have been to one state in Africa where, attached to the prime minister's office alone, there are 64 cars and 74 chauffeurs: prestige consciousness. There is the building of skyscrapers-incomplete:	prestige consciousness. As the minister must know, very serious trouble has arisen in some countries, particularly in the United States, with regard to diplomatic immunity and the major problem is not one of traffic tickets only, not one of passing through red lights or of accidents; it extends even to killing.
Prestige consciousness: we have to admit it is there, we have to understand it. I say this not only as a result of what I learned by attending meetings of the United Nations or of what I saw while in Africa; it has been confirmed by what I have read ever since then. We may not understand this attitude, but it is the product of long years when Africans were submerged by colonialism and dictatorship along with all that went with such a history. Now, as the Africans rise to independence and are able to take part throughout the world in conferences at the United Nations and so on, this feeling expresses itself. Is this not the understanding of the minister? Is this not the understanding of his African bureau?
Why then was the recommendation made that a member of the opposition, indeed a member of the smallest group represented in the opposition, should be sent to Africa in the name of the government in an attempt to find out and understand their problems,

rather than a cabinet minister or a high ranking official of the department? This question, to me, has a psychological aspect and I am afraid it is a very important one. It follows from the prestige consciousness which I have outlined. It stems from the efforts of Africans to show that they are at least the equal of the white man, if not better than the whites. I am disturbed that the man chosen for this mission is not a member of the government or a representative of parliament at top level. It is not a personal matter at all. I am surprised the man chosen should be a representative of the smallest group in this house.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs will appreciate the point I am making. I ask him whether my view is not shared by members of the African bureau of his department or by himself. If I am wrong, let him correct me, though may I say, Mr. Chairman, that I think I am correct. As a matter of fact I had this opinion driven home to me only two days ago at a reception here where there were a group of Nigerians. Because I dared to criticize them out of turn, they told me that if I was ever allowed in Nigeria they would put me on the next plane back. They do not like the white criticizing the black, this is the point I am making. I suggest the basis for a decision of the kind the minister has taken should be an understanding of the psychology of the African and of the prestige consciousness to which I have referred, and that the representative should have been chosen not so much on the basis of the knowledge and experience of the hon. member for Red Deer as on the acceptance and the prestige attaching to the choice.

I should like to say to the hon. gentleman, who has made a thoughtful contribution, that I have noted the points he has mentioned. I was aware of the problems he mentioned before a decision was taken in this case. Perhaps the hon. member will recall that one of the reasons in our minds was that the hon. gentleman in question, because of his long stay in Africa, had made acquaintance in a number of instances with personalities of great importance. This was the primary reason for the decision. We have in our African division and in the limited number of diplomatic missions in Africa, both resident and non-resident, very able officials and they will not regard the assignment as being in any way a reflection upon them, nor is it any reflection upon them. As the minister in charge of this de-
Supply-External Affairs partment I wish to say that in the African division here in Ottawa, and in the foreign service in Africa, there are officials of the highest calibre who are doing an outstanding job.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I realize that people on the opposition side who enter into this debate and are critical of the minister may lose an opportunity to be sent abroad as representatives of the government in the future.
On the contrary.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With the sole exception of myself, because the minister earlier today committed himself to sending me abroad as soon as possible. I think the hon. gentleman will now find that members on the opposition side of the house will be seeking to establish their claim to represent the government overseas by letting us know the number of years they have spent in various countries. I want to draw to the minister's attention the fact that I have spent several years abroad in England and in Europe and that I have met the heads of state of most of the countries of western Europe, and in view of the lack of experienced personnel-
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to point out that it is not so much what he did when he was in Europe as what he has done since?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is such a scarcity of talent among the hon. gentleman's colleagues that I thought I would just draw this to his attention.
I wonder at the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yet, why should I wonder? In an accident prone government every one of the members of the cabinet eventually becomes infected with the virus, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs is no exception. Travelling, as he has been for a number of weeks and months, in the stratosphere, he has finally been grounded; we have got him down to earth and he is now in communication with people on the terrestrial sphere-and this is where we want to keep him.
Earlier this afternoon the minister attempted to evade this one question which we raised yesterday, and which could have been settled yesterday had he returned to the house earlier than he did and sent out to the airport with Monsieur Henri Spaak, the distinguished representative of Belgium, one of his colleagues also interested in NATO, the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of Finance. Then he might have returned to the

Supply-External Affairs House of Commons yesterday and we could have had questions and answers on this matter and settled it promptly. But he did not do that; he came back to the house late in the afternoon. Then today he wanted to divert our attention to what he called much more important matters and he wanted to discuss the changes that have occurred in world affairs, in the country neighbouring us, and the atomic explosion that occurred in China. These, he said, were much more important matters than this particular one. Then when we pinned him down to discuss the problem that we raised yesterday, he came up with the story that the hon. member for Red Deer was on a mission abroad with regard to the safety of Canadians who are kept prisoner in the Congo.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what I said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the safety of Canadians in the Congo overrides, at the moment, some of these other international situations, important as they are. If this had been the purpose of sending the hon. member for Red Deer abroad, we would have had a statement in the house when this occurred-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what I said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -or we would have had a press release; because this minister is not reticent at all about telling us what he is doing. If you mention the word Cyprus, his breast swells like that of a pouter pigeon and he talks about the great peace keeping activities of Canada, and if action had not been taken in March there might have been serious trouble in Cyprus. You mention the United Nations and again he swells with pride and gives us a long discourse about his experience at the United Nations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
But here, when the safety of Canadians in the Congo is concerned, it is an afterthought; he said nothing about it yesterday or the day before, and there was no press release. If the safety of Canadians in the Congo is uppermost in the mind of the minister-and I think it should be-why has he not some permanent official in Africa carrying on the negotiations on which he has now sent the hon. member for Red Deer?
The hon. member for Red Deer cannot go to Stanleyville, the minister told us this afternoon. He cannot even go anywhere in the Congo, I presume; he has to go to neighbouring countries. What does he know about

these countries neighbouring the Congo, except Ethiopia? The minister raised this in order to cover up what he has been doing. I thought he would give us an exact itinerary of the peregrinations of the modern Marco Polo from Red Deer. Why doesn't he tell us exactly where he is and where he is going? He dropped out some of the points which were brought to our attention by others. Why didn't he say something about Ghana? Is the hon. member going to Ghana?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The hon. member for Red Deer is the particular man for the job; he has been in Ethiopia for 15 years and knows something about the troubles in that area. He is going to be in Cairo. Cyprus is not far away; send him there and he will bring back the information. Talk about carrying a message to Garcia. He is the man who will find out and let us know what the situation is there. sit here in the House of Commons realize the lack of ability on the benches opposite, but the people of Canada have not had this brought to their attention by the government members. These are questions
Supply-External Affairs which arise in the minds of hon. members, and I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs, now he is back on earth with us, will give us satisfactory answers.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I listened with very great interest to my hon. friend. As I indicated later in a qualification I just was speaking figuratively.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the minister. I did not hear that remark earlier this afternoon but I am glad to have it now. So it did not get under my skin at all. I am very thick skinned anyway.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend should not tell me he is thick skinned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But not thick headed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, not thick
headed; I would never accuse my friend of that. However, I do not draw any conclusion from that remark either, because I do want to keep this debate on a very high plane. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. The minister is a little muddled here. I did not say anything about members of the Department of External Affairs. Please do not confuse me with the hon. member for Villeneuve.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I know my hon. friend did not; but I am, and that is the important part of my intervention which apparently the hon. gentleman has not understood. There were good reasons for the decision which was taken. One of the reasons for the decision was that the hon. gentleman had an acquaintanceship with the area in a special way because of his long period of residence there and because he knew certain personalities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Was there no one else who could go?

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question. What particular experience has the hon. member for Red Deer had in those parts of Africa which have been listed this afternoon as the places he is visiting? Does he speak the Bantu languages?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that would necessarily be a disability. It would, of course, be helpful if the hon. gentleman could speak the language. I know my hon. friend went to Cairo the other day and had a very useful visit. He was able to draw some conclusions which were very valuable and was kind enough to give me some of them. 

But I do not think, unless I am wrong, that he speaks the language spoken there.

I would not expect to be appointed representative of the government of Canada when I do not speak Arabic and have very little experience of the area. However, I should still like to know what experience the hon. member for Red Deer has of the Congo, of Ghana and of some other areas like Kenya, for instance? Has he a close association with Jomo Kenyatta?

I dealt with that earlier. He will be seeing Mr. Kenyatta, who is head of the organization which Canada, the United States, Belgium and several other countries are counting on for assistance in connection with the situation in Stanleyville. But that was not the only reason for which the hon. gentleman was sent there. In fact it was not even the primary reason. It was because of our conversations with Mr. Spaak that this became a very useful thing for us to do, and it was done with the knowledge of that distinguished gentleman.
Now, my hon. friend asked me whether there was no other person who could have been sent. For my hon. friend's benefit-and I was not too anxious to say this-we have sent another person in connection with the particular situation in Leopoldville and Stanleyville. That person has gone to Brussels for purposes of trying, before he goes to Leopoldville, to review in particular the situation which might be expected in the period following the visit of the hon. member for Red Deer. He is a person in the department who has had long experience, as has the hon. gentleman, in Africa and who knows some of the personalities there. I am sure hon. members will appreciate why I cannot go any further.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friends laugh. In this particular situation the lives of 26 people from Canada are involved as well as 800 others.
Do not use it as a smokescreen.

I am sure my hon. friend understands that it is not desirable to give away facts which would prejudice a very important mission which I hope will be a successful one.
My hon. friend asked me a question about the Canadian soldier in Cyprus. I regret that

my hon. friend has less faith in the United Nations than I have. I regret that he does not think the Cyprus operation has been a useful one. That is his judgment. I am sure it is not the judgment of this house. It is not the judgment of the people of Canada; nor is it the judgment of those 108 soldiers who are conferring today in the west block on peace keeping matters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the minister knows-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me answer the hon. gentleman's question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am speaking to a question of privilege. The minister, who up to this point has been unexpectedly reasonable, is now falsifying the record. I was not finding any fault whatever with the United Nations operations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The official reports which I have now seen indicate that the Canadian soldier suffered a flesh wound in the arm. However, I am glad to report that his condition is not serious. At the time of the shooting he was not on duty and was unarmed. He apparently failed to stop when challenged by a Greek Cypriot policeman, who did not recognize him as a Canadian soldier. When warning shots were fired he ran toward the Turkish sector. It was then the firing took place which resulted in the arm wound.

Mr. Speaker, today, for the third or fourth time since the beginning of this session, Bill No. S-6 entitled, An act incorporating the bank of western Canada is submitted to this house. This bill originated in the Senate, and the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) proposed an amendment thereto that this bill be not now read a second time but that it be read this day six months.
On several occasions during the discussion on this bill we pointed out that three bills for the incorporation of banks were introduced in the Senate and House of Commons.
Two were passed by the Senate, namely, Bill No. S-13 entitled "An act to incorporate the Laurentide bank of Canada", and the present bill incorporating the bank of western Canada.
Another group of citizens request this incorporation of a bank to be known as the bank of British Columbia. The Senate committee on banking and commerce has been studying this bill for several months; the Senate took no action respecting this third bank, and it does not seem at present that it intends to take any more action about it than it has in the past. We stated in this house, and clearly enough so our remarks could be understood by the members of the other place, that our work would be facilitated if we could examine those three bills at the same time, that is Bills S-6, S-13, and S-20, which deal with the incorporation of three banks.	__
The members of this house are elected by the people; they represent ridings and consequently are entitled to a minimum of consideration by the members of the other place.
Since members of the house have on several occasions expressed the wish to study the three bills at the same time, the senators should at least do something to comply with this wish.

Bank of Western Canada
But far from sitting and working to submit this third bill, the members of the other place are constantly taking holidays. The Senate sits two, three or four days and then takes a month's holiday. It sits again and takes an! other holiday. It has been adjourned for a month and today it is taking another month's holiday.
If the senators do not want to sit, they should tell us so we would refrain from sending bills for their approval, since they are not apparently willing to accept them.
What right have the senators to reject bills brought forward by the people, for the House of Commons' approval, as they are doing when they refuse to defer those bills to this house for study?
By acting this way, Mr. Speaker, I say that the other place is assuming powers which it does not have, that of blocking the passage of legislation, because those powers belong to the elected representatives of the people and not to persons who owe their appointment to the Senate to mere political partisanship.
If members of the other place want to keep on taking holidays, adjourning and not doing their work, then, in my opinion, they themselves are bringing on all the reflections cast upon their institution.
So, when members of this house express the wish to study and analyse those three bills at the same time, I feel this is a perfectly legitimate request and one which the Senate ought to take into consideration.
We have no objection to seeing the banking and commerce committee of the Senate take into serious and due consideration Bill No. S-20, an act to incorporate the bank of British Columbia, but at least let it meet for such a study.
At the rate things are now going, the Senate is not meeting and the senators are enjoying perpetual holidays. Now, how can they pass a bill if they are never in Ottawa? The House of Commons should at least remind the senators now and then that if they want the Senate to keep existing, they must fulfil their duty toward the Canadian people and toward the House of Commons.

Therefore, it may perhaps be necessary to ask for the second reading to be postponed for a year in order to give those who are supposed to send us the third bill I mentioned, more time for consideration.
Mr. Speaker, that is the reason-I want to make that clear-why we are asking to postpone the second reading of this bill until a later date.
We feel that we will then better fulfil our duty as members of the House of Commons, as representatives of the people-and I insist on the expression "representatives of the people"-because we will have all the facts before us.
To our minds, to have all the facts before us is to have the three bills, not one or two, but three.
We do not oppose second reading of the bill as such. We do not oppose the setting up of other banks in Canada. But we are against the fact that we are denied the opportunity of studying the three bills at the same time.
I insist on letting it be known, clearly, categorically, and unequivocally, so that the members of the other place might know that we do not want to be handicapped in our work with regard to private bills.
We express the wish, and I trust there is in this nothing offensive, that in the vicinity of this house our request be taken into serious consideration so that we may receive all bills bearing on corporations and new banks, in order that we may be able to do justice, not only to the members of the house who will study the bills in committee, but also to those who have submitted petitions with a view to obtaining a bank charter for they too suffer serious detriment as a result of what goes on in a certain branch of this parliament, and suffer losses through ensuing delays.
That should be taken into consideration. That is why I make this appeal through you, Mr. Speaker-for I know you have the opportunity of meeting the parties concerned-that the people from the other place send us Bill No. S-20 as soon as possible in order that second reading of the three bills on banks might be proceeded with and that they be studied in committee; thus we might give satisfaction to all interested parties who are entitled to such consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Keeping your view in mind, Mr. Speaker, may I say that in my opinion B.C. is a section of western Canada and anything affecting western Canada affects B.C. However, I shall try to abide by your ruling. Present business activity in B.C. was well illustrated by the brief recently presented by that province to the hon. gentlemen in the other place. It revealed that while the population of that part of western Canada which is B.C. is somewhat less than the population of the combined area of the Atlantic provinces, nevertheless it has a labour force 2.5 per cent greater, a labour income 55 per cent greater, retail sales 21 per cent greater, factory shipments 134 per cent greater and cheques cashed 238 per cent greater than the combined Atlantic provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I tried to make it clear that in my opinion we cannot consider this bill without taking into consideration the needs of B.C., which is part of western Canada. I think that the realities of B.C.'s international and national trade position differ greatly from those of the areas in the central provinces which are served by the existing

private banks, and there is great need for the establishment of a bank in western Canada, particularly in B.C., to serve the interests of that area.
