speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the consideration
of the estimates of the department and the agencies for which I am responsible presents unusual problems because of the reorganization which has taken place since the main estimates were tabled. The department itself has been divided into two main sections headed by two deputy ministers. The deputy registrar general is now responsible for all matters which used to be under the Department of the Secretary of State, with the exception of the translation bureau but including the administration of the Patent, Copyright and Trade Marks Acts, for which the Minister of Justice is now responsible.
With regard to that section of the department which is still under my responsibility, I have nothing in particular to report to the committee except to say that a substantial revision of the Companies Act is now being considered in the other place and will soon be ready, I hope, for study and examination by the House of Commons. The under secretary of state is responsible for the translation bureau and the national museum, which has been transferred from the department of


northern affairs to my department. He advises me also on questions of administration and financial policy affecting the various agencies reporting to me. I will enumerate those agencies later on.

At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words concerning the bureau for translations. In that service, the work load has tremendously increased these last few years. I think that the development of government activities, the extension of parliamentary works and the increase in the number of royal commissions, account in great part for this situation.
The bilingualism policy adopted by the government is another important incidental factor. The simultaneous interpretation branch was also literally snowed under. Under such conditions, it is no wonder that the quality of the work has fallen down, in certain cases, in spite of the dedication of the staff to whom I must pay tribute. We are taking various steps to remedy that situation. The salaries have been increased and an office was set up in Montreal to make recruitment easier. We hope to be able to add at least 50 new employees to the staff during the next few months. In order to promote recruitment, special courses are offered to those who would like to become translators or interpreters but who do not have all the required qualifications. The purpose is not only to increase the staff, but production must be improved and also the quality of services, and that is why we intend to proceed with a reorganization where it is desirable in the bureau for translations.
As a first step, we are now setting up a terminology centre under the direction of Mr. Pierre Daviault who is leaving his position as superintendent of the bureau of translations. We are very happy to take advantage in this way of the long experience acquired by Mr. Daviault in the field of recruiting, at a time when scientific techniques change so quickly and the translation of specialized vocabularies causes difficulties. The main purpose of this new centre will be to keep up with the evolution of specialized terminology, by consulting appropriate publications and keeping in contact with similar organizations existing in other countries and on the international level as well.
It will establish a terminology filing system, as well as a catalogue and a library of technical reference works. It will also publish occasionally glossaries of which the public

will be able to take advantage, in accordance with a recommendation of the Glassco commission.
In this way the terminology centre will be in a position to render a great many services. It will save time for translators; it will help to improve the quality of translations and standardize the technical vocabulary in Canada, in both official languages.
In short, valuable improvements have been made recently within the bureau for translations. Other reforms are initiated and I shall report on them next year.
In closing that part of my remarks I want to say that the government intends to make of the bureau for translations a fully efficient agency, because it is an essential part of our bilingualism program.

I now come to the agencies for which I am responsible to parliament. Members of the committee will remember that my predecessor, the present Minister of Transport, was responsible for the following agencies: The civil service commission, the chief electoral officer, the B.B.G., the C.B.C., the national film board, the national gallery, the archives and the national library. All those agencies still report to the Secretary of State. In addition I continue to be responsible for the centennial commission and the economic council, as I was as president of the privy council. The Department of Public Printing and Stationery now reports to me instead of to the Minister of Defence Production. Finally, the Canada Council reports to me and not to the Prime Minister as it used to do.
I am quite sure that all members of the committee will agree that it would become quite bothersome if I were to make separate statements on each individual agency. Therefore I propose to make only three general statements covering them all and outlining the main programs and plans which concern them individually. Such a progress report will, I think, give a much better idea of what government and its agencies are trying to do in those fields, and will provide to the members of the committee some kind of general framework which will put them in a much better position to appreciate what is being done or contemplated for the immediate future. I hasten to say that this approach is not intended in any way to restrict hon. members' right to discuss as long as they wish each individual item of those estimates.
In this first statement I intend to refer briefly to two different agencies which are
Supply-Secretary of State quite unrelated to each other, the economic council and the civil service commission. When the estimates of my department, those of these two agencies and of the chief electoral officer, have been approved, I propose at the proper occasion to make two other general statements, one on the cultural policy of the government and on the so-called cultural or information agencies, the other on centennial preparations and the centennial commission.
The economic council of Canada held its first meeting on January 14 and 15, 1964, in Ottawa. The government is very proud to have succeeded in securing the services of Dr. John Deutsch, Louis Couillard and Arthur Smith to act respectively as chairman, vice chairman and full time director of the council. We also feel that the other 25 members of the council represent very well all the major components of the private sector of our economy. In addition I am satisfied that the council has succeeded in getting an efficient and devoted staff.
All the members of the committee who are interested in the activities of the council have already, I am sure, carefully read its annual report which was tabled on July 15. I do not have very much to add to the information contained in that report. In its first year of activities the council has concentrated its attention on the development of its internal organization, the building up of a solid research base and the establishment of liaison arrangements with similar provincial agencies and the main private sectors of the economy.
The highest priority in this program of work has been assigned to the preparation of the first of its annual reviews of Canada's medium and long term prospects and problems. This review will deal with the tasks and goals of the Canadian economy for the next five years up until 1970. It will be published in December.
Work is also under way on a number of other projects and studies. Working committees on economic growth and problems of adjustment, on labour management relations, on productivity and on industrial research and technology have been established to facilitate the development of this work. The council is sponsoring a national conference on labour management relations to be held in Ottawa next week. This conference will mark a new approach in the promotion of labour management consultation and will be based on research studies which are being specifically prepared by leading experts. In addition, the council is sponsoring a number of special studies by outside experts. All this work and

Supply-Secretary of State analysis will provide not only the basis of advice to the government but also valuable information to the private sectors of the economy which will help them to make their own decisions and forward plans.
The council's initial investigation and information of advice, have been given an unprecedented degree of independence. The bringing to bear of an informed, independent appraisal of the medium and long range implications of government policy may be one of the most useful consequences of the establishment of the council. This independence will not be weakened or destroyed by any action of this government.
No problem area which bears on Canada's economic future is beyond the scope of the council's inquiry. How it examines these problems is entirely within its competence. There is a provision in the act for the government formally to seek the advice of the council on specific problems or government policies having long run economic implications. In deference to the work load undertaken by the council in its initial year of operations, the government has not yet sought advice from the council on specific policies. The council's first annual review will provide a useful, over-all perspective within which future references by the government could be made.
The council has held meetings with the provincial economic and productivity councils and expects to meet again with these bodies after the publication of its first annual review. The chairman of the council has assured me that on the basis of the review every effort will be directed at developing effective and practical means of consultation with the appropriate provincial agencies in regard to all matters of common concern.
The council has met six times so far this year, and there have been numerous meetings of the various committees. The diligence with which the council, under the active chairmanship of Dr. John Deutsch, has applied itself to the task set for it, is to be commended. This is obviously a working council. The fruits of that labour will shortly be available to parliament and the Canadian public in the form of the first annual review. The government looks forward with confidence and high expectations to this first substantive publication of the council. This document and the subsequent recommendations will carry the weight of expert analysis and the collective wisdom of a body whose members, in their own right, are leaders in the private sector of the economy.


Thus we feel that we have a good piece of legislation and a good, dynamic council which will soon be in a position to make an essential contribution, through its research, its projections and recommendations, to the development of economic planning in Canada.
In presenting the estimates for the current fiscal year, the civil service commission wishes to report to the committee on a number of activities which should be of particular interest, either because they represent significant changes in traditional programs or are innovations designed to solve new problems encountered in providing staff and services for the departments and agencies of the civil service.
The commission has established a new salary administration plan, and a systematic appraisal program for senior officers in the civil service. It is also constructing a manpower inventory of managerial and professional resources. This inventory will be kept up to date and will provide a ready and quick means, consistent with the merit principle, for meeting the needs of all departments and agencies, at the senior levels. It is hoped that a purposeful career development program can be evolved for senior officers to ensure that there is a reservoir of competent managerial talent, available to the public service sufficient to meet the increasingly demanding requirements which rapidly changing socioeconomic conditions will create.
Following a preliminary analysis of requirements for senior managerial staff, it was concluded that a much more significant development program is required for senior officers than the one-month course given annually over the past several years. The commission instituted this year a four-month senior course in public administration held in residence at Carleton Place. Some 30 officers, carefully selected from departmental nominations, were admitted to the course last spring. This course was assessed as being extremely valuable to the participating departments, and the commission has now established this program as an annual activity in response to the demands of the senior officials in government departments throughout the public service.
As a result of recommendations made by the preparatory committee on collective bargaining, the government concluded that a substantial change in the civil service classification system would be required as prerequisite to the introduction of collective bargaining and arbitration. On the request of the government, the commission has undertaken a

Supply-Secretary of State
classification revision program intended to produce class structures based, in the main, on occupational grouping designed to apply horizontally throughout the civil service. The bureau of classification revision has been established to undertake this project. Another unit, a classification branch, has been established to meet the day-to-day requirements in relation to the present classification system; this unit will work on a diminishing scale, as the new classification system is put into effect.
With the advent of collective bargaining, the commission has been giving careful consideration to its future role in staffing the civil service. The commission, like industry and commerce, is faced with problems in recruitment created by the increasing demand for more highly trained technical and professional staff, not to mention managerial staff. Early in 1965 the commission hopes to be in a position with staff and facilities to compete effectively with other institutions, both public and private, for a fair share of available manpower resources. The commission is convinced that unless it takes an aggressive attitude in this competitive market the service will be at a serious disadvantage in meeting its commitments to the public over the next five to ten years.

Mr. Chairman, at the end of September 1963, the treasury board authorized the staff and appropriations required for the launching, early in 1964, of a central program for the teaching of the two official languages to public servants.
The commission then proceeded to the appointment of a co-ordinator and an advisory committee, the renting of premises, the installation of a language laboratory and the hiring of four teachers.
The first stage of the program was completed during the first semester of 1964, when three courses in French and one in English, the length of which varied from ten weeks in the case of part-time courses to four fulltime courses, were given to 42 civil servants designated by the different departments and grouped on the basis of scientific tests.
After taking into consideration the past experience, the program was developed further and strengthened during the summer of 1964.
Before it opened in September the school was provided with an additional laboratory, the number of classrooms was increased to
10, and the personnel to eight teachers and two supervisors.
It is anticipated that in January 1965 the total staff will include 20 full time and ten part time teachers.
During the second phase of the program the school will thus be able to accommodate, during a 12-month period, approximately 700 students who will attend courses of various lengths.
The commission is basing its program on some very solid facts, one of which is that, in selecting teachers, establishing facilities and choosing programs, the commission must measure up to the standards required in this highly specialized area of teaching a second language to adults, according to the resources available in our country at this moment for this purpose.
There must be a small number of students in each classroom, because it appears that a class of eight to ten students, instead of 15 as had previously been figured, offers the best possibilities of profitable exchanges between teacher and students.
It is also important to note that no single formula can be applied universally and that the program, as a whole, must offer a diversity of courses which can benefit various classes of students.
Therefore, a complete training from the elementary and intermediate levels will produce a meagre success if it is not on a full time basis, or at least of a half-day duration, with all the equipment required during an initial phase of intensive training lasting as much as four months. This would be followed by a second phase of a duration of several months, with a less intensive on-the-job training.
That is why courses of a half-day duration will be given only, in general, to more advanced students or as an extension of the intensive training.
They will also be offered to those employees whose work only requires a very limited knowledge of both languages, as well as to senior officials who have a great ability to learn, but who really cannot stay away from their duties. If such courses were ever made available to all civil servants, it would rather be with a view to sustaining the general interest, pending the establishment of entirely satisfactory facilities.
The commission is convinced that in order to be useful, a training program must be supported by supplementary arrangements designed to provide graduates with a real

Supply-Secretary of State opportunity to make good use of and to improve their newly acquired knowledge. Those arrangements will include personal incentive programs to be applied at home, but also opportunities for work under bilingual conditions.
The commission will be pleased to lend a hand to such departments as wish to help in setting up such conditions. In the meantime, it is imperative that, during the training stages, each group be composed of students who have approximately the same education and aptitudes for learning.
Consequently, it is necessary to group, under a single and vast training program, the greatest possible number of students, in order to provide the required number of homogeneous classes. That is why applications for registration should be pooled, and dealt with as much as possible from a coordinating centre staffed with travelling teachers as well as resident teachers, rather than through a series of independent departmental programs, which would be less efficient and more costly.
A word, now, about some of the practical measures taken by the commission in the matter of selection of bilingual personnel to meet the requirements. Apart from competitions for positions where a knowledge of both languages is a necessary requirement, it has now become the practice to allow extra marks for the knowledge of both languages in the case of competitions set up to fill positions where this knowledge would be useful. However, this practice continues to allow candidates with a knowledge of only one of our two official languages, to become eligible for a position. On the other hand, since bilingualism is part and parcel of the merit principle, not only with regard to some particular positions but in the areas where there is a general shortage, the knowledge of both languages is required in the case of some competitions to recruit more than one employee. This is being done with the deliberate intention to increase the number of bilingual employees, in areas where there is a shortage of them.
All examinations have now been analysed, especially those which are used to recruit university graduates, in order to ensure that they are in conformity with the intelligence and general knowledge tests and that they are not based on learning peculiar to a particular system of culture or teaching. The commission, however, keeps in close contact with teaching and training institutions, in order to be able to assess accurately and

fairly the various kinds of levels of training which exist throughout the country.
Finally, steps were taken to ensure that examining boards are composed of members who can hold a complete interview in that of the two official languages which the candidate has chosen, and who can also assess his education, his experience and his possibilities of success.

I want to make it clear, however, as I have already said on several occasions, that we do not intend to impose our general program of bilingualism on the civil service. We believe that it cannot be successful without the sincere and full co-operation of the civil servants and their associations. That is why we intend to consult with the staff associations before implementing important phases of our major undertaking. Above all, we do not want to impinge upon existing rights or to create new sources of discrimination while attempting to eliminate existing unfairness.
A great number of civil servants have already understood their new challenge and in many cases they have taken special training courses on their own initiative and at their own expense. Thus we are quite sure that the civil servants will accept a government program of bilingualism, not reluctantly and as a concession but as an opportunity for their own cultural enrichment, which will enable them to better serve all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I understand it, the minister's plan is to have us, if we are going to make any remarks, make them on the agencies of his department that have been covered. For something like the C.B.C. or the national film board, which he will cover later, he would request that we touch on those matters later after he makes an introductory statement. Some of my colleagues want to make some remarks about the translation system. I wanted to place several questions on the record and perhaps the minister could answer them later.
I am very interested in knowing whether there is going to be any relationship in timing and discussion among the Department of Finance on its preparing a white paper in relationship to the budget, the Department of Trade and Commerce in the preparing of the document that it puts forward every year on private and public investment in Canada, and the major publication, I take it to be-it is an annual publication-of the Canada economic council. The reason I am

interested in this matter is to discover what kind of liaison or relationship has developed in this particular field, which I think is a delicate one. We would like to assume, in one way, that the economic council is operating on its own. It seems to me it has the personnel, the staff and the independence the minister talked of; but there is also the problem of which I am sure the government must be aware, and it would certainly be exploited in this chamber if there was a great discrepancy in the analyses and the projections. I would assume that this would be solved in the main by the fact that the economic council would be projecting into the future much more than these other agencies have done. Yet I think it is quite apparent that every time we get a budget it is the projection out of the white paper which is the analysis of current conditions, and the public and private investment in Canada also stands in the same way. I would appreciate it if the minister could fill us in a bit on how these major publishing efforts, two by government departments and one by a new agency, are going to be dovetailed.
The next question I wanted to raise is this. I did not get the early part of the minister's remarks in French, but I wondered whether he made any distinction in connection with the problem that I have heard about from some civil servants beyond Ottawa. I refer to the relative disadvantage of the outside service to the service inside, or at Ottawa, in relation to this whole question of bicultural-ism and training. I suppose it is very apparent that most senior civil servants, in particular, would be willing to improve their prospects by taking courses of training; but it is also apparent that anyone who is in the west is going to have much less chance to use, in practice, socially or any other way, his other language, particularly if it is the French language.
I am just wondering what plan the government has to meet this particular problem. I have had it put to me by people who are, for example, in charge of offices in Winnipeg and the lakehead and who are in the years when one could expect further promotion- perhaps promotion to Ottawa-that they are at an obvious disadvantage. I would be interested if the minister could tell us anything about plans to compensate for the disadvantage from which the outside service suffers.
The other question I want to raise-and I do not believe the minister touched on it at all-is the problem relating to the Com-
Supply-Secretary of State panies Act and the fact that so many companies are behind in the annual reports required by the Companies Act. I know that before the committee of the other place the gentleman who is in charge of Companies Act registrations and the bureau in the minister's department gave evidence to the effect, it seemed to me, that the Companies Act requirements, in so far as the posting of information and keeping it up to date is concerned, was observed more in the breach than in actuality. This is a matter that has interested me for some time. I would like to know what practical steps are being taken to correct this situation, how well it is coming along, whether it is being met by some future streamlining of the department, or whether there is an attempt to get more personnel and deal with it in that particular way.
The other point I wanted to put to the minister by way of a question was to ask him about the planning function within the ministry itself. I think this is a fair question to raise since the minister is responsible for the economic council. One of the matters which confuses those of us who are in opposition is that we will read a speech which we can appreciate by, say, the Minister of Forestry dealing with economic planning or ARDA and its future. Then we will read addresses given by the Minister of Industry which indicate that he is also involved in the whole question of economic planning, the direction of investment and the development of incentives. We take for granted that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce are also operating in this field. Consequently some of us tend to feel that there may be a profusion of responsibilities in the whole area of economic planning and direction. We welcome the new agency, but what is the actual setup within the ministry to deal with this question?
I ask this question particularly because for several years there have been comments in business circles to the effect that businessmen would prefer some minister who has over-all responsibility in this matter. It seems to me that since the government gave the Minister of Forestry the particular powers which he has and developed the Department of Industry, on the surface at least there has tended to be some fragmentation.
I think it is worth while making the political observation that the Prime Minister is not filling in the gap so far as the public and this house are concerned. I think it is a fair comment to say that the present Prime Minister in general economic affairs and

Supply-Secretary of State economic planning has not been thus preoccupied either in the house or in the speeches which he gives across the country. There may be reasons for this, of course, but it does lead us to ask the question whether there is an inner cabinet which deals with economic matters. For example, how does it function, is there any scale of priority and what is the relationship of this group with agencies such as, for example, the Bank of Canada? It may be that bringing this matter before the minister will be fruitless because many of us are tending to forget that he is an economist and see him rather as some-I hate to use the word "cultural" figure because I am afraid that Canadians who think of culture do not think of economists. I think that is a fair comment. I think the minister might be candid enough, since he has some relationship with the economic council, to enlighten us somewhat on this particular subject.

I hasten to say that this is not to the disadvantage of the minister, quite the contrary, because if we consider the scale of values, in its application to man, cultural values come before economic values. Now, having been appointed as Secretary of State, he climbed a rung and found a field where he could distinguish himself.

Mr. Chairman, I am proud of the role played here by our group since 1962. At that time, there was practically no question of simultaneous interpretation or bilingualism in the committees, and yet today there is an increasing tendency to bilingualism.
There is no doubt that the program submitted to us today by the Secretary of State deserves our commendation. The Secretary of State looked after first things first. It is obvious that if we want translators and interpreters, a terminology must first be created.
Until all those who are engaged in translation or interpretation may acquire this terminology, which will be developed through the publishing of dictionaries, as was mentioned by the Secretary of State, translation or interpretation will continue to play a secondary role.
But with a real terminology centre within the translation and interpretation sections, then our language will develop in its true clarity and precision.
I also appreciated the statement of the Secretary of State concerning the French courses given those who must learn that language, and the English courses to those who will benefit by learning the English

language. There are now modern methods, and I believe the Secretary of State has used them. In fact, these modern methods enable an individual who knows practically nothing of another language to speak it in an understandable way in a very short time. If these language laboratories and modern methods are used in these courses, I am convinced that the efforts will be crowned with success.
The minister mentioned staff recruiting also. In that field, recruitment now constitutes an important factor. For instance, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) tells us that the Canada Year Book, which is quite an important and valuable book, not only for hon. members but also for a great many businessmen, industrialists or tradesmen in Canada, has been published in French two and a half or even three months- in fact it was in June and the English version had been published in January-that is nearly five months after the English version, then one has to admit that the bureau of translations is short of translators.

speechtext:
I deserved to be called to order, but at least I said what I wanted to say.
Mr. Chairman, mention is made of the terminology centre and other means that might help bilingualism throughout the country. It will be done through this terminology centre and by means of more intensive recruiting, especially in schools specialized in those fields.
Even though we commend the Secretary of State, it must be recognized all the same that what he is submitting to us at present is only a program he intends to establish. We will be looking forward to the results of the program to appreciate its worth. Once again, we must congratulate the minister for the program which he set forth and its efficiency will be judged by its application.
In connection with translation, I would like to point out the example of Belgium to the Secretary of State. It is known that Belgium is a bilingual country where Flemish and Walloon are spoken. I had the opportunity to meet members of the Belgian legislature and to discuss with them their translation system as well as the publication of reports, votes and proceedings or the official report of the Belgian legislature. I have been impressed by one point in particular, namely that in Belgium all the proceedings, all the minutes and all the reports are published in only

Supply-Secretary of State one booklet. Texts in both languages are printed in the same booklet in two different columns opposite one another. On one side you have the version in one language and on the other you find it in the other language.
I asked a Belgian member of parliament the reason why the publication of reports, speeches, laws, etc. was made in both languages in the same booklet, and I was told that in publishing bilingual reports in only one booklet or section of a publication, reports and records of the debates had unavoidably to be published simultaneously in both languages.
In addition, I was told that any reference in one language to a certain page of Hansard or of the Votes and Proceedings is sure to be found on the same page, in the other language, because the original and the translation are printed side by side. Since the Secretary of State wishes to improve the bureau for translations, he might consider this so as to hasten the publication of the French version of the committees' minutes and proceedings.
Let us take, for instance, the proceedings of Senate or house committees. Very often the French edition is published two to three weeks and sometimes one month after the English version.
It would be much more convenient if the two versions were published simultaneously, since that would enable us to compare both versions, because errors of translation and interpretation do occur.
Sometimes a speech is given in French and, when translated into English, it no longer has the same meaning. It should also be possible to compare other works, for all those who may wish to do so or at least are interested in learning both languages. Then, having the two versions side by side, they could become more bilingual. I think the system used in Belgium, for the publication of all committee proceedings and all speeches made in the national assembly, could be adopted in this country.
Mr. Chairman, once again, I should like to refer to the translation or interpretation system and, incidentally, to the bilingual stenographers also, about which I have a special comment to make, if the matter comes under the Secretary of State.
Mr. Chairman, I notice that the Secretary of State nods his head indicating that it does not come under him. Perhaps I could come back to that when we discuss the Speaker's estimates.

Mr. Chairman, the Secretary of State also referred to the Canada economic council. I listened to his remarks with interest and what struck me is that after a year of existence, the Canada economic council is now preparing a review of long and medium term projects of economic development and that it is also involved in the development of consultation facilities.
If after one year of existence, the Canada economic council is preparing a review of legislation on long and medium term economic expansion, I feel that the job that was entrusted to it will never be carried out, because when that review of projects is over and when the time comes to implement them, the economic development will have evolved so much that they will have to start another review.
Therefore, what is needed now under the present circumstances, is not long and medium term programs, but the fulfilment of the possibilities of the country and an economic advisory council which will act, not by drafting programs but by looking into the possibilities of development that exist in this country.
It is on the basis of Canada's natural resources and physical possibilities that the economic advisory council must operate, rather than on the basis of long term programs, for in this day and age evolution is so rapid, progress so advanced that if we do not keep up with the times, we will never succeed through long term planning, in catching up with progress, fo - we will constantly be in the process of preparing plans and programs which will never be implemented.
Since the end of the war, we heard about policies and projects planning. But, when a project has been planned and is ready for implementation, a commission of inquiry or a committee is appointed to adapt this policy planned five or six years previously.
I feel that the economic council should concentrate on the adaptation of our economic, financial, monetary and production system to our times, rather than on the planning of projects for a distant future.
Mr. Chairman, this economic council can be of tremendous service if it acts upon existing data, this country's capabilities, and not upon projections into a rather distant future, because at that time, progress will have developed to such an extent as to require a complete review of the said policy.
In conclusion, I should like to tell the Secretary of State that his speech on bilingualism within parliament and the civil service can only meet with our approval, at least

in its main lines, and we hope that he will try his best so that this program may be carried out completely.

I have just a brief general comment I want to make, Mr. Chairman, and then I want to refer to one aspect of a matter about which the Secretary of State spoke in his opening remarks. My general comment arises from the interest there was in the country, during the last election campaign, about the prospect of the Liberals, if they came to power, going in for economic planning. We have been watching for that ever since the government took office. We have found ourselves wondering which minister it was who was going to head up economic planning and do something about it.
The Department of Industry was set up, and we thought perhaps the minister of that department was to be our economic planner. We looked in vain in that direction. Some people thought it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but he is not the economic planner. Neither is the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Forestry makes speeches on economic planning outside the house, as do some others. It appears now, at last, we have found the head of economic planning in this government, namely the Secretary of State. I noticed the hon. member for Port Arthur was a little concerned as to which of the minister's aspects were going to come out on top, his cultural side or his economic side. It may be that we have in the Secretary of State Canada's C. P. Snow. I suppose I should find some way of putting that into French, but I will leave that to the translation bureau that comes under the minister's department.
At any rate, I hope that this minister will not disappoint us the way others have done, by just giving us a certain amount of talk about economic planning. If I may say so, I thought there was a good deal of sense in some of the things he said in his brief remarks tonight. I certainly hope that the work of the economic council of Canada, and the other agencies to which the minister referred, will be pushed ahead. I know the minister from
Supply-Secretary of State days long since gone by. I believe his basic philosophy is sound. I just hope he will find some opportunity of putting that philosophy into practice.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I said there was one aspect of a matter about which the minister spoke which I wanted to ask him a question or two. I refer to the translation bureau which comes under the Secretary of State. I noted with interest what he told us about establishing a terminology centre and I also noted with interest the indication that it is hoped at least 50 new employees will be added to the translation bureau in the next little while. I certainly hope this latter aim will be achieved. Other members have spoken about the significance of all this in relation to the program for bilingualism. I should like to look at it from the standpoint of the problem that some of the employees of this department have to face.
I am thinking particularly of our own translators who are in these booths at the foot of this chamber and who are having to translate what we say from one language to the other all the time the house is in session. As the Secretary of State knows, I am sure, those persons are employees of his department and not employees of the House of Commons. This means, therefore, that they may be assigned to work that is being done here in the House of Commons, but they are called upon also to work in a good many other places. Accordingly if at the same time the House of Commons is sitting the other place happens to be sitting as well, and if there is a peace keeping conference or a conference on mentally retarded children-

Some of us have been wondering just where this peace keeping conference could do the most good. Yes, perhaps it may be at the federal-provincial level, but there are times when peace keeping ought to be brought into the floor of the House of Commons. There may be times when the Liberal party or the Conservative party could use it within its own ranks.
The point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman, is that it seems inevitable that when a group of employees can be called upon to work in any one of a dozen different places, without any planner like the Secretary of State planning these various conferences so that they do not overlap each other, the problem created for the employees is impossible. The Secretary of State may say that

Supply-Secretary of State this problem will be solved when these 50 new employees are taken on by the translation bureau. This may be so. However, I suspect that concurrent with the employment of these 50 new employees in the translation bureau- and I take it this means increasing both the number of interpreters and the number of translators; I am using "translators" to refer to those who translate the written word into the other language and "interpreters" to refer to those in the booths who interpret orally for us-the amount of work to be done will grow and probably in the end the strain on these employees will be just as heavy. In the light of all this there is a question to be faced as to whether the people who work for the House of Commons ought to be brought directly under the House of Commons itself.
It is true that this is an unusual year when measured by the length of the session. It is now in its 184th day, far beyond anything in the past, but the likelihood is that House of Commons sessions will continue to be rather lengthy. The likelihood is that committee work will grow, and in view of all this I suggest there is a case for the interpreters-maybe this applies to the translators as well-who work for the House of Commons to be employed by the House of Commons. At present they are employed by a department outside the house and are sent all over Ottawa, indeed anywhere away from Ottawa on assignments where the government requires interpreting done.
I would like to hear the Secretary of State comment on this problem this evening. If he does not agree with my suggestion, then will he tell us why interpreters who work for the house ought not to be in a separate section attached to and under the control of the house itself?
Before sitting down may I refer to another subject in this general field. As I have already said, I am interested in the announcement that a terminology centre is to be established, with the present director of the bureau of translations as its head. I am interested in the reasons which the minister gave for the establishment of such a centre, but could he tell us whether any research is being carried on by his department, the translation bureau or any other branch of government, into automatic or electronic translating devices? I speak now of translating rather than interpreting. In some parts of the world a great deal of research is being conducted into this sort of thing, and the day may come when by using such devices translations will
fMr. Knowles.]

be produced faster than they can be done now.
In conclusion I would like the minister to tell us what hopeful word he has for the people who are in the glassed in booths at the foot of the chamber who interpret our words as we speak.

I appreciate the hon. member's having brought this subject before the committee. Some of us take an interest in the working conditions of house staff, and those of us who do always notice the volume of hours which the interpreting staff have to devote to the performance of their duties in this chamber. I endorse the previous speaker's observations that there is a constant conflict between their work here and assignments outside the house to committees, boards arid conferences.
I suggest there should be greater engagement of freelance interpreters for such outside work. This would relieve the tremendous stress and strain on the interpreting staff of the house who, if they had an opportunity to speak on their own behalf, would certainly tell us that their hours of work this session have been extremely difficult for them to handle. They have done so without complaint and they deserve our immediate and earnest consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to add a few brief comments about the estimates of the Secretary of State.
First, I would like to congratulate the minister for the wonderful job he has done up to the present in the field of bilingualism, which is, we all agree, rather complicated and difficult. He endeavoured to increase the number of bilingual officials in parliament and in the various departments, by giving them the opportunity to study the other language of the country.
However, I feel I must make a few remarks on this matter in order to call his attention to a danger with which I am concerned.
When the various departments will give promotions in the coming months or years, when they will have to take into consideration the qualifications of the various candidates for those promotions, I feel that the people who will be in charge of this selection will need to be very careful not to consider as bilingual a person who, for all practical purposes, can understand or write only a few words of French.
However, if the intention is to play somewhat on words, and lead us to believe that in

future there will be only bilingual civil servants when the Anglo-Saxon group has had an opportunity to learn a little French to meet the requirements of the various departments, in order to prevent the promotion of perfectly bilingual French Canadians, then I think that we will have fought in this house for nothing.
We noticed that in the past, English speaking civil servants, in the house and in other departments, were promoted over the heads of fully bilingual French speaking personnel, and following criticism made on several occasions the departments decided to teach French to their officials in order to avoid criticism henceforth in matters of promotions.
I believe that this had to be said, and the minister may be assured that we will always be on the alert and ready to defend the interests of those who could be so wronged. I may give him the assurance that each time we have the opportunity-and I hope the situation will not be repeated-we shall be ready to bring to the attention of the minister these cases which may occur.
The minister has reported on the activities of the economic council of Canada. Some weeks ago, I asked him when he expected to table a report on the activities of this agency which has already been in existence for a year. I was surprised by his silence in this regard.
On the other hand, I imagined that an agency working silently had perhaps a better chance to produce something positive, but when I see the work done by the Atlantic development board, I unfortunately cannot reach this conclusion-I was going to use the phrase "unfortunately I cannot reach the conclusion"-since the board which has not worked silently and was granted some funds, has already done a good job in the Atlantic provinces and invested some money in hydroelectric developments, and also in many other projects, in conjunction with the provinces concerned. We therefore have here an agency which, besides doing planning, sees to it that all imaginable possibilities are realized in the imediate future.
I wonder if, since we decided to create it, it would not have been preferable to grant more authority to this economic council, so it could show results more quickly. I am wondering how it has been operating during the last year. Did it consult the provincial authorities without whose co-operation no planning can be established, because the provincial governments own their natural resources. I think that it is a delusion to endeavour to attain some measure of success
Supply-Secretary of State without considering the views of the different provincial governments. Did the members of this agency visit the areas of our country? Did they hear the representations of the agencies which are responsible for the economic development of the various regions in order to ascertain the research which was carried out in those various areas and avoid a duplication of work, expenses and energy?
It would be interesting to know the answers to all those questions because when they visit those regions, those gentlemen could realize the local possibilities and also the developments we can expect from them.
Within the Department of Industry, there is of course what is called a regional development agency. Does that agency achieve a concrete job? Has it the approval of the provincial authorities for such work? Does that agency of the Department of Industry come into conflict with the projects now under consideration by the economic council of Canada? Those are some more questions to which we would like to get answers.
In any case, the minister can be assured that we will wait, I should even say with impatience, for that first report of the economic council because it will indicate whether we made a mistake in setting it up and if we can hope that the work already carried out is liable to produce concrete achievements enabling us to form an opinion on the efficiency of the decision taken on that matter.
Of course, reference was made a while ago to the need of personnel in the translation offices and also in the French language reporters division. Having been myself on several committees, I was in a position to notice the progress made in those fields, but unfortunately, on many occasions, due to the fact that several committees sat at the same time, we sometimes had to do without the services of bilingual reporters. I think that even if the minister often said that he made real efforts to hire some, we are still wondering why it is that his efforts were not successful. It is clear that it is difficult to train such a qualified personnel in a relatively short period, but I think that the problem has been pointed out to the authorities for more than two years. In my opinion the time has come to present tangible achievements in this field.
As the minister dealt with only two particular points, I shall limit myself to them. There are other subjects under his jurisdiction and in which I am interested. I shall

Supply-Secretary of State wait therefore till the right moment comes to discuss them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words to say with respect to the estimates of the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamon-tagne.)
Like the previous speaker, I would like to congratulate the minister for promoting bilingualism in all the federal departments and I would also like to encourage him to do even more.
The main purpose of my intervention is to correct the impression that bilingualism started here in the house only after the arrival of the Social Credit members, a group which now calls itself the Ralliement Creditiste.
In 1957 when I was elected for the first time, my colleagues of the province of Quebec and myself endeavoured to increase the use of French on parliament hill. I for one made a list of the various signs appearing in numerous places inside the centre block as well as outside on the hill, and I asked the then responsible minister to make arrangements so that exclusively English signs be replaced by bilingual signs, which we can see today nearly everywhere.
Another example indicating the interest we took in this matter is the fact that the then minister of defence production, Hon. R. O'Hurley, was the first to publish in French the report of the Department of Defence Production.
He also appointed to a crown corporation a French speaking Canadian as president. He also took several other steps to spread the use of French in Ottawa.
In his statement the minister says that French courses and English courses were given to civil servants to enable them to familiarize themselves with either of the official languages of the country. I would like to know the number of civil servants who take full-time French or English courses.
I also ask the minister to be very explicit on the marks granted in civil service commission competitions to those who speak the two official languages of the country.
I should like him to tell us also, in the case of a vacant position in a community where French only, or vice-versa English only, is spoken, whether an application from a bilingual employee would be considered?
Before I conclude my remarks, I should like to remind the Secretary of State that during the election campaigns, the 1963 campaign especially, Liberal candidates in the


province of Quebec promised a special bonus to bilingual employees. I should like to know whether this project is still in the minister's mind and if so, when does he expect to carry it out? Furthermore, if he does not intend to pay special bonus to bilingual employees, what are the reasons today for his change of policy?

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased to hear that the Secretary of State is interested in the problem of making bilingualism available to many of the senior civil servants who otherwise would not have the opportunity of becoming bilingual. There are in Ottawa a great many senior civil servants who are very much afraid of the situation that has been created by this French-English problem. The bilingual atmosphere, for which perhaps members of the Ralliement Creditiste can take some credit, has spread to the degree that to be promoted within a department you must be bilingual.
As one who cannot speak French, I know that if an elevator operator is hired and he cannot speak one word in English, very soon he becomes bilingual. It is a fact that though he is not bilingual when hired, within a few weeks he will be bilingual or he is just not going to get by and will not know when it is dinner time, in some cases. Therefore he becomes bilingual. I have found this is very true with most of the bilingual jobs with which I have been in contact. You telephone the Department of Agriculture, for instance. I presume the people you talk to are bilingual. I have often talked to three or four people before I got one to whom I could put a question and get an answer. They are bilingual all right, but it certainly must be in another language; it is not English.
The point is that because of the geographic situation in Canada those bilingual people who are going to get these jobs have to come from an area where French is taught and is the native language. It is very easy to pick up a second language by association, but it is very difficult to learn a second language through study. For this reason I am very happy that the minister has decided that courses will be made available, so that the fact we want to have, in a federal sense, a bilingual nation will not mean that those who are not raised in the province of Quebec under the French educational system will be eliminated from obtaining all types of jobs.
We may say that this will not happen, that we are not going to discriminate; but

I wonder how often we discriminate in regard to many of the jobs posted for the civil service, particularly those jobs that call for bilingualism when bilingualism is not a necessity, an advantage or even to be desired. There are many, many jobs in this country where it is no advantage, unless it is for personal satisfaction, to be bilingual. We often hear civil servants in Ottawa saying, "Oh, I cannot be promoted", or "There is no point in my trying for that job". I know an engineer who experienced this difficulty a couple of weeks ago with regard to the Department of Industry. This man had held civil service jobs in the past and has three or four degrees. He said, "Well, look at the posters". We went through them all, the bilingual requirement was the main aspect of the qualifications required, and he had no opportunity to obtain one of these jobs. He certainly would have been ill advised to apply, because he is not bilingual. It seems to me that many of the jobs in the Department of Industry did not really require a person working in most parts of Canada to be bilingual.
I think it is also a fact that this is not a bilingual nation. I believe we in this house well understand the scope of bilingualism, its advantages and the fact that the federal government is pledged to allow the use of either official language and, much better, both official languages; but it is not necessary to have two official languages. This, of course, raises another problem. I receive a considerable amount of correspondence in French because a great many of my constituents are French and write to me in that language. While I have a small knowledge of that language, my translation is very bad and very often it becomes confused and I have difficulty with this correspondence. To be fair to the Secretary of State, my most recent translations are being done by his executive secretary, who was kind enough to offer his services because there is just no service provided in the department. I think this is a service that should be provided.
While we are thinking about the translation department and the simultaneous translators here and bringing them into the staff of the House of Commons, we should realize that there must be established a branch which will handle translation. I telephone the minister's department and talk to his translation branch. The official there is either very bilingual himself and does not understand the situation, or has an odd interpretation of what are government matters. If he thinks I am sending over correspondence just because I would like to 20220-622
Supply-Secretary of State have it translated, I have news for him. This is not the purpose; it is government business that comes to me as a representative of government. I believe it is the responsibility of somebody to provide this type of translation service for members of parliament, because there is no consideration of having to be bilingual and in fact you do not have to be able to read and write to be a member of parliament-although sometimes it helps. It is not really necessary to be bilingual; but I believe your constituents-and I am very serious about this-if they write to you in either of the official languages, have a right to expect an answer in the language in which they write. But this is not possible because of the unavailability of a translation service.
The minister will have to provide us with the same type of schools that he is willing to provide for the senior civil servants, or he will have to provide us with a translation service that will translate this correspondence for us. I have gone to the messenger service, to the simultaneous interpreters here, and to the protective staff; I have cornered pretty nearly everyone who speaks both our official languages. I am very happy to say that they are most obliging people and will translate a letter for me. But when you have a thick sheaf of papers they begin to wonder whether they should undertake the job, and in most cases they do not. As members of parliament I think we have an obligation to our constituents, and if we have only one French speaking person in the riding we should be in the position where we can reply to him in his own language. This can only be done if we have a translation service.
I think we have to draw the line somewhere; I do not think we are going to be able to re-educate all the people in Canada. I am not opposed to that, and I am not really opposed to our making this a bilingual nation; but I do not think we are going to do it by the back door. We are not going to do it by forcing the civil service to be bilingual, without our having enough courage to decide to institute a national education system in this country that will provide French and English tuition to all the people of Canada.
If we offer a job requiring bilingualism we are eliminating applications on the part of people from nine of the ten provinces for that job. I think that French Canadians in the federal field are being very unreasonable in asking that everything be translated into French and that all the vacancy postings in the civil service be also put in French. I say that

Supply-Secretary of State because this means that only people from Quebec are able to take advantage of any civil service job.
I might say that the four or five years I spent in high school learning the French language would not give me any bilingual qualification in any shape or form-in the same way as I learned Latin and then tried to talk to Italians; that was just about as silly. The minister has a very big department with surveys taking place, and so on. I do not think our national education is in such a bad way and the minister says he believes we can progress. But if he is not prepared to do what I suggest, it seems to me that we will have to be very careful-and I hope the minister will say whether he is willing to exercise this kind of care-to see that civil service job postings are not loaded in favour of bilingual candidates when bilingualism is not a requirement for the position concerned. There are some civil servants in the gallery now who are bilingual and others who are not. I think every one of those postings which is slanted in favour of bilingual candidates is directed toward a particular person who is in mind for the job. If it cannot be open the posting might just as well not be put up at all. So we will either have to be very careful about using this bilingualism weapon in the civil service or we are going to have to go much further than that and provide equal opportunity for all Canadians.
I know some will say they would not accept that or that it cannot be done. I see several French Canadian members of parliament shaking their heads, indicating they are not in favour of that. All they are really saying is: We want an advantage over all other Canadians. They are not saying they want equality. They are saying: Give us a damned big advantage which we want to hang on to.

speechtext: That is not so.

speechtext:
Someone says no. With the exception of a person from my area, or Timmins, Sudbury and perhaps a few other ridings in eastern Ontario, a person from Ontario would have no possibility on coming out of high school of having any French to enable him to speak intelligently with a French Canadian. He could not pass any type of examination in the French language. Are these people not good enough to be in the civil service? What about the people in Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Nova Scotia or Newfoundland? Are they not going to be able to qualify for positions in the civil service? That is what it amounts to if this

practice is used indiscriminately. I think the minister should give consideration to this matter.
I would also make a plea that the translation branch and other branches for which we in the House of Commons have assumed responsibilities and over which the Speaker has some limited jurisdiction be transferred to a special branch. One of these days we are not going to have any oral translation at all. If hon. members would check they would find that on many days just two people are running the House of Commons simultaneous translation system all day long. Where are the others? Perhaps one will be in Montreal, two or three at a committee meeting somewhere, another out of town. They are greatly understaffed. The international regulations of their union will not allow them to carry on this type of operation for very long. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, if we had 50 we would only be bringing their number up to strength. Some extension must be made in the near future. I would think that the amount of translation being done in the committees branch now is four to five times as much as when I first came to parliament. I think that is also true with the federal-provincial conferences which are taking place these days; a simultaneous translation system is provided there. Therefore I suggest these people should be given some protection.
I should just like once again to commend the minister on the job he has undertaken in the retraining of senior civil servants, because I think that is important. It is something from which some benefit can flow. If the type of inequality to which I have referred is watched and the government is willing to provide bilingual training where necessary, this will lessen many of the fears of those who find they have reached a dead end street, particularly in Ottawa, as far as promotion is concerned as a result of the emphasis which is being placed on bilingualism today. I do not know whether we are smart enough or young enough to meet the other requirements, but I should like to see members of parliament given an opportunity of attending classes similar to those attended by civil servants. In my own particular case there is a small segment of my riding the people of which speak French only, and it would be of great advantage if we members of parliament were given the rudiments of the language, although it is a fact that the simultaneous translation system has elimi-

nated to quite an extent the previous motivation for learning the second language.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words following the speech made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). When he said that in some departments he had to contact three or four officials before he found anyone who spoke English, I thought he had addressed himself to the government of the province of Quebec.
Amongst other things, he claimed that certain high officials and technicians of the Department of Industry were reluctant to seek promotions because they are not bilingual. I should like to point out to him that if there is a department in Ottawa which is not bilingual, it is surely the Department of Industry. Indeed, I think that only one out of 13 high officials is bilingual in that department. At least, the person in question has a French name. I suppose that, once again, the hon. member has no grounds to complain.
I should also like to say that if the hon. member feels that French Canadians are discriminatory when they seek to have their language recognized, he must admit that very little has been done in the past hundred years about the problem of the French language. If the consideration given to the question now is slightly annoying to some members, they must understand that the present emphasis is due to the fact that precious little was done about the recognition of French during all those years.
The present situation is quite surprising for them, but they must not be worried. If, in a few months or a few years from now, the question creates general interest-that is the great difference between the past and the present-it will be less obvious and requests such as those which are made today will pass unnoticed.
I should also like to say a word about the civil service commission. However, my remarks will not deal with the question of French, since others have made the usual authoritative representations in that respect a while ago. Consequently, there is no need for me to add anything to what they said.
However, apart from the fact that the Laurendeau-Dunton commission will certainly find out problems coming under the civil service commission in the fields of French language and bilingualism, I think it would be desirable also in certain cases to 20220-622J
Supply-Secretary of State inquire into the civil service commission itself.
I know that this commission is not under political control and that its employees are all competent and render unusual services to the country. However, in certain cases, uncommon as they may be, we noticed minor irregularities and discriminations in the advertising of some competitions requiring certain qualifications, which were already known by a few, of course.
Nevertheless, I feel it would be a good thing if the minister would become interested in that problem and ask qualified persons, outside the civil service commission and completely independent in that field, to make a special investigation.
I am personally aware, for having inquired myself from certain government agencies, that it was realized that-unknowingly no doubt-there were certain discriminations, not necessarily concerning languages, but rather proficiency, residence of the candidate, his record, and finally for different reasons, it seemed to me that a little discrimination may occur in some cases.
I feel that many civil servants would be pleased to learn of an unbiased inquiry, in order to appraise, first of all, the duties and also the classification and promotional methods affecting civil servants.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the next few minutes I would like, as some of my colleagues have done, to comment on bilingualism in the civil service, in various federal departments and crown corporations.
It has been urged not very long ago that bilingualism be enforced in Canada. I would like to ask especially the ministers to reply when possible in French to any letter written in French. Very recently I wrote in French to a minister and I received a reply in English.
If the good intentions expressed this evening by the Secretary of State are to be put into practice, federal ministers should start by setting an example.
We should also like to remind the house that in Canada, as everybody knows, French Canadians make up about 30 per cent of the total population. Now, it would be interesting to learn-not to raise the cry of discrimination, but just to find out-what is the percentage of French Canadians, at present, among those holding jobs in the public administration. The thing is that, as the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out, it may be easier for French Canadians to be perfectly or simply bilingual. It would be interesting, then, to find out if, with this greater aptitude, French Canadians hold a proportion of jobs in keeping with the percentage of this country's French Canadian population.
I would also like to recall to the attention of the minister, whose estimates we are considering tonight, that last summer several delegations toured the national gallery and some other places coming under his department; on such occasions, we could meet only one bilingual employee able to answer in the language of the delegations' members.
I would therefore ask the minister concerned to kindly put into practice, as soon as possible, the good intentions he has shown us tonight. It is excellent to mean well, but we are expecting still a lot of realizations in this field.
These last years only, that is for two years now, much has been said in Canada on bilingualism. And while, during those two years progress was made in that direction, the accomplishments should at least be put into practice, not in obliging all Anglo-Saxon Canadians to learn French, but in showing respect, by using its own language, to an important section of the Canadian population, that is the French Canadian population, in order that the latter be treated fairly, and
[Mr. Caouette.l
in its dealings with the departments and the various crown companies, receive replies in its own language.
Mr. Chairman, I would be happy if the minister, one year from now, could outline the accomplishments of his department in that field.

I agree fully with him that the interpreters, especially in the last year or so, have worked under very difficult conditions. I said in my opening statement that we were now reviewing the whole situation of the translation bureau, and for the time being at least I am certainly including the interpreters as a very important part of that bureau. This does not mean there will not be any change in the near future. I think it would be very helpful, Mr. Chairman, if we were allowed another few months to review the situation of the translation bureau in order to be able to provide the house with the best service possible, and these very devoted civil servants with the best working conditions possible.
So far as automatic translation devices are concerned, the hon. member may be quite sure that we are looking into all possible means of dealing with this difficult problem of translation in order to find the most effective solution for the needs of the government and parliament.

As far as the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) is concerned, I would like to tell him that my statement tonight is but a very partial report on the program on bilingualism we are considering. Last December I made a statement on these programs in general and that statement answered the questions raised by the hon. member. As soon as decisions are reached in this connection, I will be pleased to submit a new report to the committee for I do not believe that this is the last time my estimates will come up for consideration. I will then be pleased to submit to the house a new report which I am sure will show that the present government does not intend to disown the promises it made to its supporters.
Supply-Secretary of State

To conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say three things to the hon. member for Timiskaming. First of all, if we have a recess I am quite sure that he will be welcome at the school. Second, as I said in my opening statement we, as a government, have a program for increasing bilingualism in the whole civil service, but we do not want to impose that program on the civil servants. Finally, I think the hon. member should only begin to worry when French Canadians have more than their proper share of jobs in the civil service.

SHIPPING-REPORTED LACK OF SERVICE TO CARIBBEAN AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and arose from a statement by a Canadian commercial counsellor in the central American area to the effect that Canadian exporters were missing the boat because of the lack of adequate shipping between Canada, the West Indies and the central Carribean area. I could not agree more with what Mr. Lemieux said.
I asked the minister whether the government would consider taking steps to encourage the expansion of shipping to that area so that more frequent sailings could lead to the development of our trade with the West Indies and Central American areas. Knowledge of and interest in these respective areas must precede the development of trade. I think that is generally conceded. In addition there must be frequent sailings, because an importer anywhere in those areas needs to know how he can get the goods he needs quickly, and if there are frequent sailings he can get them quickly.


In the general context of my remarks I also include the necessity for good air freight cargo service to and from the Caribbean area. We in the maritime provinces, and I think also in the province of Quebec, have long realized the importance of the British West Indies to Canada, and the historic trading relations within certain limits and certain products. I have always felt that I have found here in Ottawa that the rest of Canada have their heads deep in the sand with regard to the potential of the West Indies area to Canada. Here is an area, with notable exceptions, with a British tradition, an area which is come into independence and maturity, an area which inevitably will be nothing more than an appendage to the United States economy, unless we in Canada are at long last prepared to take the hand of friendship which has been proffered so often to us by those people, and to develop our commercial contacts with the West Indies.
What we must do is have some form of economic union, get as large a portion as possible of the West Indies into the Canadian dollar sphere and out of the sterling bloc, so that we can trade with them and send our winter vacationists there without affecting our balance of payments. It is in this connection that the mutual usefulness of the West Indies and Canada does exist. Mr. Lemieux does a service to Canada in pointing out the need for more frequent sailings. The Department of Trade and Commerce spends money and does a great deal of research to develop trade. I want to say that here is an area where the department should seriously consider providing some form of subsidy to private shipping to encourage more regular runs to that area. If this were done for four or five years, trade would have grown to the point when a subsidy would no longer be necessary. It is the old story of what comes first, the chicken or the egg. The shipping has to be there before the trade can grow. In that period of time, if it is to be made profitable for private enterprise, there must be assistance from the government. It is in the national interest. It helps our trade to grow and helps to improve our relationship with this important area, one which is all the more important because there has recently been a federation of these so-called outer seven, St. Kitts, Barbados and five others.
This is a country which will be looking for independence after 1965 and which will be looking to Canada for assistance in the development of national trade. I hope we will be prepared to meet them at that time. The

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
prime minister of the Bahamas said to me last year that he found Canada had never shown much interest in the Bahamas in the past. I hope this will not continue. I know that in Britain Mr. Gordon Walker, as well as his predecessor in the Conservative government Mr. Duncan Sandys, and Mr. Nigel Birch have expressed again and again their desire that Canada should be willing to participate on a tripartite basis in the assistance and in the administration which is given to that area by Britain as it becomes more independent. I think that in this direction lies a great future for Canada. We must not lose our opportunity to develop a type of economic union with the only area which remains as a potential warm country, not tropical, but all the year round warm country, with which we can have some form of economic union as it develops.
